---
title: "Using the Shiny app"
---

The `singlehitapp` package lets you run a singlehit analysis in your web
browser without writing R code. You load data, fit the models, compare them,
add bootstrap confidence intervals, and download plots. You can also browse
the QMRA wiki experiment library and test whether experiments can be pooled.
Everything the app does calls exported singlehit functions, so its results
match the package's results.

## Install and launch

The app is a separate package stored in the `app/` directory of the singlehit
repository. Run these lines once at the R console:

```r
install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("seanthimons/singlehit")      # singlehit 0.3.0 or later
pak::pak("seanthimons/singlehit/app")  # the app
```

Then start it whenever you want to use it:

```r
singlehitapp::run_app()
```

The app opens in your browser. While it runs, the R console is busy. To stop
the app, close the browser tab and press Esc (or Ctrl+C) in the console.

If you are working from a clone of the repository, run the app against the
source code instead:

```r
setwd("app")
source("dev/run_dev.R")
```

## Analyse one dataset

The tabs run from left to right. For a single dataset you use Data, then Fit,
Compare, Bootstrap, Plots, and Explore.

1. **Data.** Upload a `.csv`, `.tsv`, or `.txt` file with one row per dose
   group, or press **Use Ward rotavirus example data**. The file needs the
   columns described in [Input data format](../index.html#input-data-format).
   If the app does not recognise the column names, choose the dose, positive,
   and negative columns from the menus. The table shows the data that the
   other tabs will analyse.
2. **Fit.** Choose at least two models (exponential, beta-Poisson, and the
   slower exact beta-Poisson) and the significance level, then press
   **Run analysis**. The tab shows the dose-trend test, the parameter
   estimates, and the goodness of fit. This step does not bootstrap.
3. **Compare.** Read the primary recommendation first. It combines each
   model's absolute fit with the chi-squared deviance comparison. The
   assessment table below gives the details. The consensus vote is marked
   *Experimental*, so do not use it as the main result.
4. **Bootstrap.** Set the number of replicates (default 1,000) and an
   optional random seed, then press **Run bootstrap**. The exact beta-Poisson
   model has its own, smaller replicate count because it is much slower. The
   bootstrap runs in the background, so you can use other tabs while it works.
   Each model has a progress bar, and **Cancel** stops the run. When it
   finishes, the tab shows percentile intervals for the parameters and
   effective doses, and confidence bands appear on the Plots and Explore tabs.
   Use the same seed to get the same intervals again.
5. **Plots.** Show all fitted models in one panel (the overlay), one panel per
   model, or a single model. Confidence bands appear in the per-model and
   single-model views after a bootstrap; the overlay never shows bands. Set the
   width, height, and resolution, then download the plot as a PNG.
6. **Explore.** Build your own plot with
   [esquisse](https://dreamrs.github.io/esquisse/) by dragging variables onto
   the axes, colour, and other settings. Under **Data to explore**, choose the
   observed dose groups, the fitted curves, or the residuals. After a
   bootstrap, **Draw confidence bands** creates a ribbon plot of the fitted
   curves on a log dose axis. To hover and zoom, turn on "Use {plotly} to
   render plot" under Options.

## Browse the QMRA wiki library and test pooling

Pooling has its own path through the tabs: Data, Library, Pooling, and then
Fit.

1. **Data.** Press **Use QMRA wiki sample workbook**, or upload a QMRA wiki
   `.xlsx` workbook with a "raw data" sheet. The bundled sample holds 18
   experiments; the full workbook is not distributed with the app. A workbook
   opens on the Library tab and leaves the current dataset unchanged.
2. **Library.** Filter experiments by pathogen group, pathogen, outcome, dose
   unit, host, exposure route, strain or isolate, and preferred model. The plot
   draws each experiment's preferred model on a log dose axis. You can split it
   into panels (facets) and colour it by any filter field except pathogen. Dose units
   differ between studies, so compare curves only within one unit. Curves
   reported by the wiki only as parameters are drawn dashed.
   - To analyse one experiment, choose it and press **Send to Data and Fit**.
     Experiments that singlehit cannot fit, such as those with fewer than
     three doses, say why instead.
   - To test pooling, choose two or more experiments under **Pooling set** and
     press **Test poolability**.
3. **Pooling.** Before the test will run, you must answer **Why do these
   experiments belong together?** For example: same pathogen, host, route, and
   outcome. Decide this before you look at any results. Then press
   **Run poolability test**. The app blocks the test for data problems, such as
   mixed or missing dose units, an experiment the wiki has already pooled, or
   duplicate counts. Differences in pathogen, host, route, outcome, or strain
   produce only a warning. The results show the likelihood-ratio test, each
   experiment's own fit against the pooled fit, and the wiki's own pooled
   entry if one exists. A test that does not reject pooling is not evidence
   that the experiments are equivalent.
4. **Send pooled data to Data and Fit** makes the tested set the current
   dataset, so you can run Fit, Compare, Bootstrap, and Plots on it. Counts at
   doses that the experiments share are added together. On the Plots tab you
   can colour the observed points by experiment, strain, host, route, or
   outcome.

Every pooling run is recorded in a session log with the rationale, any
warnings, and the p-values. Download it as CSV for your records. The log
counts how many tests you have run, because none of the p-values are adjusted
for multiple testing.

The Pooling tab also has an **exploratory** section. It runs every pairwise
test as a heatmap and searches for groups of experiments. Treat what it finds
as a hypothesis, not a result. A pooling set chosen from it, or contained in a
set you have already explored, is marked *data-informed* because its test is
biased toward pooling. The
[pooling article](https://seanthimons.github.io/singlehit/articles/pooling.html)
explains why.

Neither the checks nor the test can detect two entries that report the same
subjects. For example, experiments 108 and 139 in the sample have identical
counts at six of their eight doses. Pooling them would count the same
volunteers twice.

## Reporting problems

Report bugs and confusing behaviour on the
[issue tracker](https://github.com/seanthimons/singlehit/issues). Include:

- the tab you were on;
- what you clicked or entered;
- what you expected to happen and what happened instead;
- any error message; and
- your data file, if you can share it.
